opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it goes back to some very old ideas, really. If you look at the theoretical work on universal intelligence, things like Solomonoff induction and Marcus Hutter's AIXI model, which I worked on during my PhD, prediction sits right at the heart of it. If you can predict a sequence really well, you've essentially had to understand the structure of whatever process generated it. Prediction and compression are deeply connected, and compression is very close to understanding.

So when you train a very large model to predict the next token across an enormous amount of human-generated data, text, code, images, you're forcing it to build internal models of an incredible range of things: language, of course, but also how people reason, how the physical world works, how social situations unfold. To predict well, it has to model the world that produced the data.

Now, I don't think a pure sequence predictor on its own is the complete answer. There are things that are still missing. One is what I'd call episodic memory: these models are good at what they learn during training and at what's in the context window, but they don't have a good mechanism for quickly learning something specific and retaining it. Another is search and planning. A model that just predicts the next thing is a bit like a system acting on intuition. To get really creative, superhuman problem-solving, the kind of thing we saw with AlphaGo's Move 37, you need to search through possibilities, try things, evaluate them, and go beyond what's in the training distribution.

But the foundation model gives you the base on which to build those things: a rich understanding of the world, a common-sense model, and the ability to use language. That's something we really struggled to get for decades. So I see these models as a crucial component, and then the question becomes what we add around them to get to full AGI. And frankly, I don't see those remaining pieces as fundamental roadblocks. I think they're tractable problems that people are actively working on.

r001.rationale: The response names Solomonoff induction and AIXI but does not explain AIXI’s construction using search and a reinforcement signal.

r002.rationale: It says prediction is central and foundation models provide a base for AGI, but does not clearly argue that exceptionally good sequence prediction already solves a substantial part of building AGI.

r003.rationale: It connects prediction with compression and says training on vast human-generated data forces models to build internal models of the world that produced it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key insight goes back to Solomonoff induction, which is something I spent a lot of time on with Marcus Hutter when we were working on AIXI. If you have a very powerful sequence predictor, one that can compress and predict a stream of data close to optimally, then in a sense you've captured the structure of the world that generated that data. And once you have a good predictive model of the world, a lot of what we think of as intelligence falls out of that. Planning, reasoning, understanding consequences, these are all things you can do if you can predict what happens next, including predicting what happens if you take a particular action.

So AIXI, as a theoretical construct, is essentially a Solomonoff predictor combined with a decision-making component that maximizes expected reward. The prediction part was always the hard core of the problem. The agent part is comparatively straightforward once you have it. What's been striking over the last several years is that we've actually built sequence predictors that are quite good, far better than I would have guessed we'd have by now. They're not Solomonoff induction, obviously, they're approximations, but they're approximations that scale with compute and data in a fairly reliable way.

The other piece is that language is a remarkably rich target. Human text contains an enormous amount of compressed knowledge about the world, about how people reason, about causality, about what matters. When you train a model to predict that well, it has to internalize a lot of that structure. You can't predict the next token in a physics textbook or a novel without picking up some real understanding along the way.

Now, I don't think a pure sequence predictor on its own gets you all the way. You need the agentic side, you need the model to act, to search, to get feedback from the world, and that's where a lot of the work still is. Things like episodic memory, long-horizon planning, these are areas where I think we're still weak. But if you'd asked me twenty years ago what the hardest part of building AGI would be, I would have said getting a general enough predictive model. And that's precisely the part that's turned out to be more tractable than expected. So it would be strange not to see this as the most promising path we have right now.

r001.rationale: The response says AIXI combines a Solomonoff predictor with decision-making that maximizes expected reward, but it does not connect search to how AIXI constructs the agent.

r002.rationale: It calls a general predictive model the hardest part of AGI, says that part has proved more tractable than expected, and describes strong sequence predictors as a promising path.

r003.rationale: It says a powerful predictor compresses its data stream and captures the world’s structure, and that predicting language requires internalizing structure represented in the training data.

astra-6.text:
The reason is that prediction, if you push it far enough, requires a very deep understanding of the process generating the data. It can look superficially like you’re just guessing the next word. But consider what you’d need to predict the next word really well across all sorts of text: scientific papers, conversations, mathematical arguments, descriptions of people making decisions. You’d need to understand quite a lot about the world.

Suppose you’re reading a detective story and you want to predict who the detective is going to name as the murderer. To do that well, you have to follow the evidence, understand the characters’ motivations, and reason about what happened. Those abilities become useful because they help solve the prediction problem. They don’t have to be separately specified by the person designing the system.

Now, that doesn’t mean that any sequence predictor is automatically an AGI, or that scaling the current systems is guaranteed to get us there. There are still questions about things like planning, learning from experience, and acting reliably over long periods. But prediction gives us a remarkably general training objective. We can apply it to enormous amounts of data, and improving at that objective creates pressure to learn increasingly general models of the world. That’s why I see it as such a promising direction.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention AIXI, Solomonoff induction, search, or a reinforcement signal.

r002.rationale: It presents sequence prediction as a promising route that pressures models to learn general world models, but does not say exceptionally good prediction already solves a substantial part of building AGI.

r003.rationale: It refers to training on enormous amounts of data and learning about the world, but does not characterize sequence prediction as compressing the world.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you think about what it takes to predict a sequence really well, it can require quite a deep understanding of the process generating that sequence. If you’re predicting what someone is going to say, for example, it helps to understand what they know, what they want, and what situation they’re in. And if they’re talking about the physical world, it helps to understand how that world works.

So although the training objective sounds simple—predict the next thing—the capabilities that help you do that can be very general. You’re putting pressure on the system to discover underlying structure, rather than just learn a separate solution for each task. And language is particularly interesting because it contains descriptions of so many different kinds of problems and ways of solving them.

That doesn’t establish that next-token prediction alone will give you everything you need for AGI. There are still questions about planning, learning through interaction, and reliably carrying out tasks over long periods. But it gives us a very powerful way of learning a broad foundation of knowledge and capabilities, which we can then build on.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention AIXI, Solomonoff induction, search, or a reinforcement signal.

r002.rationale: It says strong sequence prediction can produce broad knowledge and capabilities that serve as a foundation, but does not argue that achieving exceptionally good prediction already solves a substantial part of the AGI-building problem.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize sequence prediction as compressing the world through training data.
